Abstract
This paper presents a novel machine learning-driven approach for designing and optimizing multi-band patch antennas 
tailored for next-generation Internet of Things applications in 5G and 6G wireless communication systems. Recognizing 
the limitations of traditional antenna design methods, this work leverages the power of ML to enhance antenna per-
formance and design efficiency. We investigate various ML algorithms, including Decision Tree, Random Forest, ANN, 
KNN, Extra Tree, CatBoost, Gradient Boost, and XGBoost, for predicting antenna characteristics. Notably, the CatBoost 
algorithm demonstrates superior performance, achieving 77.4% accuracy in predicting antenna return loss. To validate 
the efficacy of this approach, a multi-band antenna operating across the 3.5–7.8 GHz, 8.5–10.2 GHz, and 11.8–15 GHz 
frequency bands was fabricated and evaluated. Results demonstrate a good agreement between predicted and meas-
ured performance, highlighting the accuracy and efficiency of the ML-driven design methodology. This approach holds 
significant promise for accelerating the development of high-performance antennas for a wide range of applications, 
including Wi-Fi, Fixed Wireless Access, Wideband Aeronautical Intranet Communications, IoT devices, Industrial IoT, smart 
cities, and remote monitoring systems.
Article Highlights
•	 A novel machine learning-driven methodology is presented for the design and optimization of multi-band patch 
antennas, addressing the increasing demand for efficient and high-performance antennas in next-generation 5G 
and 6G IoT applications. This approach significantly reduces antenna design time and computational resources by 
minimizing reliance on iterative simulations.
•	 A multi-band antenna operating across the frequency bands of 3.5–7.8 GHz, 8.5–10.2 GHz, and 11.8–15 GHz was 
successfully developed and tested, demonstrating strong agreement between predicted and measured results. The 
CatBoost machine learning algorithm exhibited superior performance in predicting antenna return loss, achieving 
high accuracy, speed, and reliability with low error rates.
•	 This antenna design methodology, applicable to various IoT applications including Wi-Fi, Fixed Wireless Access, Wide-
band Aeronautical Intranet Communications, Industrial IoT, smart cities, and remote monitoring, has the potential to 
revolutionize antenna development for next-generation wireless communication systems.

1  Introduction
Antenna design has gained significant importance in recent years due to its crucial role in developing effective wireless 
communication, IoT devices, and other applications reliant on electromagnetic signal transmission and reception [1]. 
Various antenna designs for IoT applications have been proposed, each featuring specific characteristics to enhance com-
munication capabilities. A mono-cone antenna with ultra-wideband (UWB) characteristics operates from 2 to 20 GHz, 
making it suitable for IoT applications [2]. Another design focuses on wearable IoT devices, operating in the 2.4 GHz ISM 
band, and incorporates human tissue models and bending effects [3]. Multi-band IoT antennas improve connectivity by 
reducing interference and supporting various communication protocols [4]. A Minkowski fractal patch antenna offers a 
miniaturized structure and operates at multiple frequencies for GPS, radar, and 5G [5]. A dual-band, two-element MIMO 
antenna system operating in the frequency range of 26.5–27.1 GHz and 39.15–40.69 GHz proposed for 5G IoT applications 
[6]. An IoT antenna supporting 5G and Wi-Fi operates in the 3.4–3.6 GHz and 5.725–5.825 GHz bands with omnidirectional 
radiation patterns [7]. An IoT antenna covering C, Ku, and K bands, with tri-band operation at 7.1, 12.8, and 20.3 GHz, 
is suitable for future security and satellite applications [8]. Traditional antenna design methods have been effective for 
specific problems but often involve extensive simulations and manual optimization. However, the rapid advancement of 
ML techniques has opened new avenues in antenna design, offering exciting opportunities to unlock the full potential 
of this essential technology [9]. Numerous researchers have experienced the transformative impact of ML in antenna 
domain. In [10] authors explored using ML to optimize a double T-shaped monopole antenna, achieving a prediction 
error of only 2.90% compared to HFSS simulations. In [11] it is found that the Random Forest algorithm outperformed 
SVR and kriging in high-dimensional antenna modeling. In [12] improved circularly polarized base station antenna 
performance using ML and data augmentation. In [13] authors proposed an ML optimization algorithm to reduce the 
computational cost of electromagnetic simulations. In [14] authors introduced an efficient KNN method for antenna opti-
mization, showing significant computational speed improvements. In [15] authors evaluated ML in predicting antenna 
responses, emphasizing the impact of training dataset size. In [16], optimized a microstrip line-fed dielectric resonator 
antenna using ML for the 1.59–2.26GHz, 3.1–3.87GHz, 5.25–6.91GHz band. In [17] authors reviewed ML and deep learn-
ing for various antenna applications, highlighting their feasibility and advantages. In [18, 19] authors discussed using 
ML for antenna design optimization, emphasizing reduced simulations and high accuracy. In [19, 20] authors reviewed 
ML applications in antenna design and optimization, noting reduced computational expenses. In [21] authors proposed 
ML methods for developing traveling wave antennas and robust antenna design. In [22] used ML to predict UWB fractal 
antenna responses, demonstrating fast optimization and effective modeling. The integration of ML into antenna design 
holds the promise of revolutionizing antenna optimization, leading to enhanced performance, improved efficiency, and 
reduced design times [23, 24]. Machine learning, a branch of artificial intelligence, offers powerful tools and algorithms 
capable of automatically learning from data, identifying patterns, and making accurate predictions [25]. By leveraging 
large datasets and advanced algorithms, ML can optimize antenna designs by considering various characteristics, con-
straints, and performance metrics. This enables engineers to explore new dimensions of antenna performance optimiza-
tion, surpassing traditional design limitations.

2  Methodological framework for integrating machine learning in antenna design
Traditional antenna design methods have numerous limitations, such as inefficiency in exploring large design spaces, 
reliance on simplifying assumptions, time-consuming iterations, and difficulty in managing complex structures and opti-
mization goals. To overcome these challenges, researchers and engineers are turning to ML and optimization algorithms. 
ML, a subfield of artificial intelligence, enables systems to learn from data and improve without explicit programming 
as shown in Fig. 2. By training algorithms on labeled datasets, they can recognize patterns, make predictions, and gen-
eralize to new, unseen data. This automation and predictive power can significantly enhance antenna design, leading 
to faster design cycles and improved performance. Combining ML with traditional methods pushes the boundaries of 
antenna performance and efficiency.
The initial phase of antenna design involves conceptualizing, designing, and simulating a microstrip antenna using 
HFSS [30], followed by rigorous performance assessment and iterative refinement if necessary. A dataset is generated by 
varying design parameters and operating frequencies, and pre-processed through normalization, feature engineering, 
and data augmentation. Essential Python libraries (e.g., NumPy, Pandas, Matplotlib) are imported for data handling and

2.1  Significance of return loss
Return loss measures how well an antenna or transmission line matches the system’s impedance, ensuring efficient power 
transfer from the source to free space for effective wireless communication [24]. It is defined as the ratio of reflected 
power due to impedance mismatch to the incident power, usually expressed in decibels (dB) as shown in Eq. (1) [36]:
A high return loss indicates efficient power transmission to the load, while a low return loss signifies significant power 
reflection back to the source [25]. High return loss minimizes signal loss, increases effective radiated power, and improves 
overall system performance, making it a critical parameter in antenna design, testing, and optimization. ML can help 
uncover the relationship between return loss and other factors, such as antenna geometry and operating frequency. 
Accurately predicting return loss can help optimize antenna designs, leading to better impedance matching and reduced 
power reflections, which can significantly enhance the performance of IoT antennas.
To integrate the antenna design with machine learning and address the complexity of this problem, a diverse set of 
machine learning algorithms were employed. A summary of these algorithms is shown in Table 1.
3  Optimizing antenna design with machine learning solutions
3.1  Stage 1: Developmental stages of antenna design and optimization
The antenna design process unfolds in four stages, with intermediate steps illustrated in Figs. 4 and 5, and geomet-
ric measurements mentioned in Table 2. The antenna measures 25 mm × 32 mm × 0.8 mm and constructed using an 
FR-4 (Flame Retardant Type 4) substrate. Throughout all design stages, the substrate thickness remains 0.8 mm, with a 
dielectric constant (εr) of 4.4 and a loss tangent (tan δ) of 0.02. In the initial stage, depicted as Step 1 in Fig. 4, the design 
features a typical square patch antenna with an 8 mm radius semicircular slot. In Step 2, a vertical slot is introduced on 
the left side of the patch. Step 3 incorporates an upper horizontal slot into the structure. Finally, in Step 4, vertical and 
horizontal slots are added at the lower edge of the patch, completing the proposed design.
When comparing the return loss across the various design steps (as shown in Fig. 6), the performance evolves sig-
nificantly from Step 1 to Step 4. Step 1 features wide band characteristics ranging from 3.2 to 10.1 GHz, exhibiting two 
notable bands at 3.8 and 7.7 GHz, with minimum return losses of − 25 dB and − 28 dB, respectively. Additionally, there 
is another band from 11 to 15 GHz with a return loss of − 13 dB. Step 2 shifts slightly, providing a band from 3 to 4 GHz, 
with a return loss of − 19 dB at 3.4 GHz. Another band extends from 4.6 to 9.8 GHz, featuring a return loss of − 25.44 dB 
at 7.9 GHz. Moreover, a smaller band spans from 11.19 to 15 GHz, achieving a return loss of − 21 dB at 13.8 GHz. Step 
3 refines the design further, resulting in a band from 3.5 to 8 GHz, with significant return losses at 4 GHz (− 42 dB) and 
7.33 GHz (− 34 dB). Another band is observed from 8.5 to 15.7 GHz, showing return losses of − 20 dB at 9 GHz and − 34 dB 
at 13.7 GHz. Step 4 achieves improved performance with a band from 3.4 to 7.6 GHz, exhibiting two bands at 4 GHz and 
7.1 GHz, with return losses of − 41.6 dB and − 28.17 dB, respectively. Additionally, there is a wide band from 8 to 15 GHz, 
featuring return losses of − 20.9 dB at 8.7 GHz and − 28 dB at 13.8 GHz. Overall, each successive step shows progressive 
improvements in return loss characteristics and bandwidth performance. Figure 7 illustrates the current distribution at 
various frequencies (4 GHz, 7.1 GHz, 8.7 GHz, and 13.8 GHz). The dominant mode is excited at the lower frequency i.e. 
4 GHz. Furthermore, higher order mode is excited by adding the long vertical slot. Thereby, adding one more slot higher 
order resonating mode are excited at 8.7 GHz and 13.8 GHz.

3.3  Stage 3: Machine learning model development
•	 Data Preprocessing: The dataset is prepared for ML training by cleaning, normalizing, and potentially reducing 
dimensionality. The dataset is then split, with 80% used for training the ML model and 20% for testing it [32, 33].
•	 Model Selection and Training: Various ML algorithms, including Decision Tree, Random Forest, ANN, KNN, Extra 
Tree, Cat Boost, Gradient Boost, and XGBoost applied to uncover relationships and predict antenna return loss. These

•	 Model Evaluation and Optimization: Table 3 presents the R-squared, MSE, MAE, MAPE, Fit Time and Prediction Time

The results demonstrate good agreement between measured, simulated, and predicted values, validating the ML 
approach’s accuracy. This methodology significantly accelerates antenna development by reducing iterative simulations 
and conserving computational resources, with potential applications in diverse IoT domains, including home automation 
systems, smart appliances, security systems, industrial IoT components, wearable devices, and smart city infrastructure. 
For example, in home automation, the antenna can enable reliable communication between smart devices, allowing 
for remote control and automation. In industrial IoT, the antenna can facilitate efficient data collection and transmission 
for predictive maintenance and asset tracking.

5  Conclusion
In this work, antenna is developed for IoT applications of next-generation wireless communication systems, by incorpo-
rating machine learning algorithms. The study rigorously evaluated eight different ML models, with CatBoost achieving 
the highest return loss prediction accuracy at an impressive 77.4%. This model also demonstrated exceptional speed 
and low error rates, highlighting its reliability for antenna design. The Cat Boost model also achieved an MSE of 7.73, 
MAE of 1.69, MAPE of 18.36, a fitting time of 9.146 s, model prediction time of 0.0218 s indicating high model reliability. 
The proposed antenna is tested and fabricated, showing good agreement with the simulated results. It operates in the 
band from 3.5 to 7.8 GHz with a bandwidth of 4.3 GHz, resonating at 4 GHz with a return loss of − 30 dB and at 7.2 GHz 
with a return loss of − 24.6 dB. This study underscores the transformative potential of ML in engineering applications,

Abstract: This paper presents a novel machine learning-driven approach for designing and optimizing multi-band patch antennas tailored for next-generation Internet of Things applications in 5G and 6G wireless communication systems. Recognizing the limitations of traditional antenna design methods, this work leverages the power of ML to enhance antenna per- formance and design efficiency. We investigate various ML algorithms, including Decision Tree, Random Forest, ANN, KNN, Extra Tree, CatBoost, Gradient Boost, and XGBoost, for predicting antenna characteristics. Notably, the CatBoost algorithm demonstrates superior performance, achieving 77.4% accuracy in predicting antenna return loss. To validate the efficacy of this approach, a multi-band antenna operating across the 3.5–7.8 GHz, 8.5–10.2 GHz, and 11.8–15 GHz frequency bands was fabricated and evaluated. Results demonstrate a good agreement between predicted and meas- ured performance, highlighting the accuracy and efficiency of the ML-driven design methodology. This approach holds significant promise for accelerating the development of high-performance antennas for a wide range of applications, including Wi-Fi, Fixed Wireless Access, Wideband Aeronautical Intranet Communications, IoT devices, Industrial IoT, smart cities, and remote monitoring systems. Article Highlights • A novel machine learning-driven methodology is presented for the design and optimization of multi-band patch antennas, addressing the increasing demand for efficient and high-performance antennas in next-generation 5G and 6G IoT applications. This approach significantly reduces antenna design time and computational resources by minimizing reliance on iterative simulations. • A multi-band antenna operating across the frequency bands of 3.5–7.8 GHz, 8.5–10.2 GHz, and 11.8–15 GHz was successfully developed and tested, demonstrating strong agreement between predicted and measured results. The CatBoost machine learning algorithm exhibited superior performance in predicting antenna return loss, achieving high accuracy, speed, and reliability with low error rates. • This antenna design methodology, applicable to various IoT applications including Wi-Fi, Fixed Wireless Access, Wide- band Aeronautical Intranet Communications, Industrial IoT, smart cities, and remote monitoring, has the potential to revolutionize antenna development for next-generation wireless communication systems. * Rachit Jain, rachit2709@gmail.com; R.
